title: AI Can Read The Code, But Can It Understand The Chip?
gist: A DAC 2026 roundtable (Cadence, Keysight EDA, Siemens EDA, Synopsys, IC Manage) argues agentic AI is a necessity to close the chip-design productivity gap, but it multiplies load on design-data management, NFS, compute and EDA licenses while raising IP governance and security risks. Panelists split on frontier vs. custom-trained models: frontier LLMs suffice for automating command-line workflows, but reaching better PPA likely needs models that understand layouts and waveforms.

insights.claim: Chip design customers are described as desperate rather than merely interested in AI because the gap between design complexity and engineering productivity keeps widening despite annual EDA improvements.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Structural demand driver for AI-EDA spend regardless of hype cycle.
insights.quote: They’re desperate because the gap between designs and our ability to improve keeps growing

insights.claim: Synopsys cites industry estimates that chipmakers are 2x short of the designers needed for desired new design starts.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Talent shortage underpins AI-augmentation adoption in EDA.
insights.locator: In dealing with customers, we see

insights.claim: Siemens EDA says top customers have become more realistic, abandoning push-button 'chip from a prompt' expectations and focusing on deterministic flows while managing token budgets and compute.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Expect targeted, task-specific AI-EDA deployments rather than end-to-end automation near term.
insights.locator: What we are seeing right now is there’s so much AI stuff

insights.claim: If each engineer directs 10-20 agents, load on design management systems, NFS and the number of EDA licenses needed rises 10x-20x; IC Manage cites 1,000 workspaces becoming 25,000.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Agentic design could expand EDA license and compute/storage demand—bullish for EDA vendors and data-management infra.
insights.quote: you’ve 10× or 20×’d the number of licenses you need to buy
insights.locator: An engineering project to design a chip may be

insights.claim: NFS is a chatty, slow protocol that is a constant speed bottleneck when nightly regressions launch on thousands of servers; IC Manage introduced an NFS booster to address it.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Storage/file-system acceleration for EDA is a niche benefiting from agent-driven load.
insights.locator: Then we’ve done a lot of work on the NFS component

insights.claim: Agents compress workloads in time—20 nightly-run epochs can happen in 8 hours—creating bursty compute demand and agents hogging LSF queues, hurting predictability.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Agentic EDA shifts compute demand to bursty peaks; capacity planning and cloud burst matter.
insights.locator: An interesting side of scaling the business is also velocity

insights.claim: Customers sitting on decades of design data find it scattered, of uncertain quality and hard to govern, so data management is shifting from storage to finding, organizing, securing and tracing data for AI use without leaking IP.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Design-data/IP-management vendors gain strategic relevance in the AI era.
insights.locator: Our customers have been using our solutions for almost 30 years

insights.claim: Licensed IP raises governance questions about whether it can be used to train or be passed to an LLM, and agentic memory raises questions about what is carried forward between designs.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Legal/contract governance tooling for IP in AI flows is an emerging need.
insights.quote: Because you license IP, can you train with that licensed IP? Probably not.
insights.locator: On the data management side, we see a couple of flavors

insights.claim: Panelists warn AI agents can go rogue and access restricted design data, driving demand for secure sandboxes and bounded sub-agent access controls, especially for government and offshore contracts.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Security controls become a selling point for EDA AI platforms.
insights.locator: One of the things customers are very concerned about

insights.claim: Some customers view every prompt as IP being given away and plan air-gapped on-prem AI deployments.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Supports on-prem/self-hosted model demand in semis.
insights.quote: Every prompt is an IP that I’m giving away.

insights.claim: Cadence says the trend toward air-gapped open-source models is reversing because frontier models like Claude, OpenAI and Gemini have become so good customers won't sacrifice quality, sometimes via self-hosting deals.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Frontier-model vendors gaining enterprise semis adoption; watch hosted/private-deployment deals.

insights.claim: LLMs handle Verilog well but do not understand waveform or layout data, which they have not been trained on, leaving open whether EDA firms or companies like Nvidia and AMD will build models that do.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Layout/waveform-native models are an unclaimed opportunity; watch EDA vs. GPU vendors.
insights.locator: Customers are figuring it out. Because it’s all new

insights.claim: Models are inefficient with massive design data, e.g. converting a terabyte waveform database into text at large token cost; tools must expose queryable abstractions instead.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: EDA vendors adding AI-queryable data APIs/MCP layers can capture value.
insights.locator: And the third thing is that models are

insights.claim: Cadence warns that training custom domain models on open-source bases is a cat-and-mouse game: by deployment they are about a year behind, and frontier models may obliterate the training work.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Risk to EDA vendors' in-house model investments; favors frontier-model partnerships.
insights.quote: The danger is that the frontier models will just obliterate what we’ve trained.
insights.locator: When it comes to training models

insights.claim: Keysight is pursuing a hybrid: training its own models while providing infrastructure for customers to build surrogate models in tightly constrained agentic workflows to prevent leakage.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Hybrid model strategy is emerging as the EDA vendor default.
insights.locator: We’re seeing a bit of a hybrid of that

insights.claim: Synopsys says models are weak at temporal assertions, suggesting specialized sub-domain models alongside frontier models for reasoning, and that frontier labs need to provide more trust.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Niche verification models may coexist with frontier LLMs.
insights.locator: In terms of the modeling, Chuck makes an important point

insights.claim: Panelists distinguish two goals: automating human command-line EDA work to close the productivity gap needs no trained models, but achieving higher PPA requires AI inside tools, e.g. a truly agentic, image-based place-and-route tool.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Separate near-term productivity plays from longer-term PPA-improving AI-native EDA tools.
insights.locator: So as we’ve been saying about closing the design productivity gap

insights.claim: Frontier models lack enterprise data; Siemens says this matters on RTL generation, while IC Manage counters that public RTL is abundant but public layouts are scarce.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Proprietary layout data is the moat for EDA/chip firms.
insights.locator: The frontier models are getting better

insights.claim: Cadence's AI fellow sets a bar for quantum relevance as more than 1% of semiconductor revenue and is unsure whether that is 5, 10 or 20 years away.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Skeptical industry insider view on quantum timelines.
